337.title: Upakosala and the fires (4.10–4.15)
337.hook: a student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and is never sent home; then the fires themselves begin to teach
337.howItsDone: In the traditional guru-shishya relationship, a Hindu student serves and lives with a teacher for years; many Hindus also speak of an inner guide, and of the outer teacher as one who points the student inward.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bull, the fire, the swan and the diving bird, Satyakama's four unlikely teachers. Your line was the whole world teaches. What taught you something yesterday? Week two of year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-seven.
screen: `THE BULL — THE WHOLE WORLD TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Satyakama grows up and becomes a teacher himself. And now he has a student of his own, Upakosala. For twelve years, Upakosala lives in his teacher's house and tends the sacred fires, keeping them fed, morning and evening. Other students come and finish and are sent home. Not him. Then Satyakama leaves on a journey, still without teaching him. And Upakosala, the text says, is so sad he stops eating. The teacher's wife begs him: eat something. He says no. I'm full of sorrow. And that's when the fires he's been tending for twelve years start to talk.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS TENDING THE FIRES.` → `EVERYONE ELSE GOES HOME.` → `HE STOPS EATING.`

segments.voice: The fires confer among themselves. This student has served us well. Let's teach him. And together they tell him: breath is Brahman. Ka is Brahman. Kha is Brahman. Upakosala is honest: I understand breath is Brahman, but I don't understand ka and kha. Ka means joy. Kha means space. And the fires explain that they're one: the joy that is also space, the space that is also joy. Then each of the three fires teaches him about itself, and about the sun, the moon, the lightning, the waters. Then they say: we've told you our part. Your teacher will tell you the way. When Satyakama comes home, he looks at his student and says what was said to him years ago: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Upakosala, a little embarrassed, glances at the fires. Satyakama listens, and then says: they told you about the worlds. I'll tell you the rest. As water doesn't cling to a lotus leaf, wrongdoing doesn't cling to one who knows this. And the teaching he gives is this: the person you see in the eye, that is the self, that is Brahman, deathless and fearless. Notice the shape of it. The fires teach the outer things. The teacher points inward, to the one looking out through the eyes. The story keeps both: Upakosala needed his teacher, and he needed the fires. But where everything finally points is the seer inside.
screen: `THE FIRES DECIDE TO TEACH.` · `KA IS JOY. KHA IS SPACE.` · `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` · `THE PERSON SEEN IN THE EYE.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice turns from the fire to the one watching it. Sit and settle. If you have a candle, you can light it and look at it; if not, look at any small light. Watch it for a few breaths: the flicker, the color. Then gently notice that there is someone seeing it. Don't try to find that someone. Just rest in the fact of seeing. Joy and space, ka and kha. The bell holds the time.
Upakosala and the fires. A student who tended the sacred fires for twelve years; the fires taught him about the world, and his teacher pointed him to the self within.
screen: `UPAKOSALA AND THE FIRES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the teacher within. Today, before you look something up or ask someone, pause for one breath and ask yourself first what you already know. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

338.title: The five fires (5.4–5.9)
338.hook: a king asks a proud young scholar five questions he can't answer, and the answer turns out to be the whole cycle of life told as five fires
338.carry: rain to food to seed to person
338.howItsDone: Hindu rites of passage, from conception to cremation, are traditionally performed around a sacred fire, and many Hindus understand cremation as a final offering into the fire.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upakosala and the fires, the student who tended them for twelve years. Your line was the teacher within. Did you pause and ask yourself first? Day three hundred thirty-eight.
screen: `UPAKOSALA — THE TEACHER WITHIN.`

segments.voice: A young man named Shvetaketu walks into the court of a king, Pravahana Jaivali, freshly educated and very sure of himself. The king asks: has your father taught you? Yes, sir. Then do you know where people go when they leave this world? No. How they come back? No. Why that other world never fills up? No. Five questions, five blanks. Shvetaketu storms home to his father: you told me I was educated! His father, a famous teacher, admits he doesn't know either. So the father goes to the king himself and asks to be taught. And what the king teaches him is a picture of five fires.
screen: `FIVE QUESTIONS, FIVE BLANKS.` → `THE FATHER DOESN'T KNOW EITHER.` → `HE GOES TO THE KING.`

segments.voice: Picture the sacrifice you met at the start of the week: a fire, and an offering poured into it. Now the king says: the whole world works like that. Five fires, five offerings. The first fire is the sky world up there. The gods pour in faith, and out of it comes Soma, the moon. The second fire is the rain cloud. Soma is poured in, and out comes rain. The third fire is the earth. Rain is poured in, and out comes food: rice, barley, plants. The fourth fire is a man. Food is poured in, and out comes seed. The fifth fire is a woman. Seed is poured in, and out comes a child. Then the king says the line the whole passage rests on: in the fifth offering, the waters come to be called a person. Follow it once more. Rain to food to seed to person. You are, in this picture, weather that has been offered and transformed five times. And it doesn't stop at birth. The person lives, dies, and is placed on the funeral fire, the last fire, and the cycle turns again. The next chapter describes the paths the dead take from there, the way of the gods and the way of the ancestors. Notice two things. First, a king, a warrior, is teaching a priest; the text has the king say this knowledge had not gone to brahmins before. Second, the fire is everywhere: not only on the altar, but in clouds, soil, bodies and births. The ritual became a way to see the whole world.

segments.voice: Today's practice follows the water. Sit and settle. Breathe in, and think of rain falling somewhere far away. Breathe out. Breathe in, and think of a field, a grain of rice, a vegetable, fed by that rain. Breathe out. Breathe in, and think of a meal that became part of your body. Breathe out. Then simply feel your body sitting here, made, the king would say, of offered rain. The bell holds the time.
The five fires. Sky, rain cloud, earth, man and woman, each one receiving an offering and giving something new, until the waters become a person.

339.title: Uddalaka and Shvetaketu: "you've studied twelve years — do you know That?" (6.1)
339.hook: a son comes home after twelve years of study, proud and stiff, and his father asks him one question he can't answer
339.tomorrow: the clay, the gold, the iron
339.howItsDone: The sixth chapter of the Chandogya is one of the most studied texts in Hindu philosophy; Vedanta teachers often walk students through Uddalaka's lessons one at a time.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five fires, the king's picture of the whole cycle of life. Your line was rain to food to seed to person. Did you taste the rain in a meal? Day three hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `THE FIVE FIRES — RAIN TO FOOD TO SEED TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: The front door opens. A young man comes home after twelve years away. He's twenty-four. He has memorized the Vedas. He walks in, the text says, swollen with pride, thinking himself very learned, a little stiff with it. Maybe you've met him. Maybe you've been him, home from the first year of college, correcting everyone at dinner. His father watches him for a while. And then he asks a question. Not a test of memory. One question. Today begins the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the most studied in Hindu philosophy: a father, a son, and a series of lessons that will run for the next two weeks.
screen: `HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS.` → `SWOLLEN WITH PRIDE.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The father is Uddalaka Aruni, one of the great teachers of the Upanishads. The son is Shvetaketu, the same young man the king embarrassed yesterday. The chapter begins twelve years earlier, when Shvetaketu is twelve, and his father sends him off to study with a warning: in our family, nobody is a brahmin just by birth. Go and learn. Now he's back, proud of all he knows. And his father asks him: since you think so much of yourself, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. How could there be such a teaching, sir? Sit with the question for a moment. It isn't asking for one more fact. Twelve years of facts are already in Shvetaketu's head. It's asking whether there's one thing that, once you know it, makes everything else make sense. A key, not another room. The Upanishads have a name for what that key opens. They often just call it That. And the father is gentle about it. He doesn't mock. He uses a word he'll repeat through all the lessons ahead: somya, my dear, the way you'd talk to someone you love. Then he begins to teach, with things from the kitchen and the garden: clay, salt, honey, a seed. Over the next two weeks the lessons keep coming, and nine times the father closes one with the same three words. Tomorrow, the first: a lump of clay.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS EARLIER, A WARNING.` · `THE UNHEARD BECOMES HEARD.` · `A KEY, NOT ANOTHER ROOM.` · `SOMYA, MY DEAR.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice sets down what you know. Sit and settle. Let the facts come up: your job, your skills, your opinions, what you studied. Notice how much is there. Then, one by one, set them down beside you, like books on a table. You can pick them all up later. For now, sit with empty hands, and let the father's question hang in the air, without answering it. The bell holds the time.
Uddalaka and Shvetaketu. A father and the proud son he asks about the teaching by which the unknown becomes known.
screen: `UDDALAKA AND SHVETAKETU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one thing worth knowing. Today, ask someone wiser than you what they think is the one thing worth knowing, and just listen. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

340.title: The clay, the gold, the iron — know one, know all (6.1)
340.hook: by knowing one lump of clay, the father says, you know everything made of clay: the pot is only a name
340.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers in many schools use Uddalaka's clay, gold and iron as a standard teaching example, and the clay-and-pot image recurs throughout later Hindu philosophy.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka and Shvetaketu, the proud son and the one question. Your line was the one thing worth knowing. Did you ask anyone what they think it is? Day three hundred forty.
screen: `UDDALAKA AND SHVETAKETU — THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Walk into any kitchen in India, or almost anywhere, and you'll find clay. A water pot. A cup for chai, thrown away after one use. A lamp for the evening. A plate, a jar, a tile. Different shapes, different names, different jobs. Shvetaketu has just asked his father how there could possibly be one teaching that makes everything known. And his father doesn't answer with a theory. He points at the pots.
screen: `A POT, A CUP, A LAMP, A JAR.` → `DIFFERENT NAMES, DIFFERENT JOBS.` → `HE POINTS AT THE POTS.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: my dear, just as by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known, the change is only a name, a matter of words, and the truth is just clay. In Sanskrit, the end of that line is famous: vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam, mrittiketyeva satyam. The change is a handle of speech, a name; clay alone is the truth. Then he says it twice more. By one gold ornament, everything made of gold is known; the truth is just gold. By one nail-cutter, everything made of iron is known; the truth is just iron. Think about what he's claiming. A pot is real. You can carry water in it. But pot is the name we give to a shape the clay has taken for a while. Break the pot, and nothing has gone out of existence. The clay is still there. It just doesn't answer to pot anymore. So if you understand clay, you understand every pot, every cup, every lamp, all at once, including ones you'll never see. Know the clay, and the names stop confusing you. Now the father is setting up the rest of the chapter. Over the next lessons, the clay will turn out to be something much bigger: what Uddalaka calls Being, the one stuff under every name. Hindu schools have read this line in different ways. Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, hears it as saying the many names are appearance and only the one is ultimately real. Other Vedanta schools, like Ramanuja's, hear the pots as real forms of the one clay. Both schools come back to this lump of clay.

segments.voice: Today's practice looks for the clay. If there's a cup or bowl nearby, hold it, or just picture one. Sit and breathe. Say its name in your mind: cup. Then let the name go and notice what's left: the weight, the coolness, the material. Breathe with that for a while. Then do the same with your own hand. Let the name go. Notice what's there. The bell holds the time.
The clay. Uddalaka's first example: know one lump of clay, and you know all clay; the pot is a name, a matter of words.

341.title: In the beginning, Being alone (6.2)
341.hook: the father tells his son the oldest story there is: in the beginning there was only Being, one, without a second
341.carry: it thought: let me be many
341.howItsDone: Uddalaka's opening line, 'Being alone, one without a second', is one of the most quoted sentences in Hindu philosophy, and ekam evadvitiyam is often recited as a summary of Vedanta.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the clay, the gold, the iron. Know one lump of clay, and you know every pot; the change is only a name. Your line was know the clay. Did you see past a label? Day three hundred forty-one.
screen: `THE CLAY — KNOW THE CLAY.`

segments.voice: Children ask it early, usually at bedtime. But what was there before? Before Grandma, before the dinosaurs, before the world? Every tradition has some answer, and many of them start the same way: in the beginning. Yesterday Uddalaka told his son that under every pot there's clay. Now Shvetaketu needs to know what the clay of everything is. And so the father goes back to the beginning, and tells him a creation story in about a dozen sentences.
screen: `BUT WHAT WAS THERE BEFORE?` → `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `THE CLAY OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka begins: sad eva somyedam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam. In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Sat, Being, what is. Then he takes on a rival view head-on. Some people say that in the beginning there was non-being, and Being came out of it. But how could that be? How could something come from nothing? No, my dear. In the beginning there was Being. Then comes the turn that gives us today's line. That Being thought: let me be many. Let me grow forth. A single wish, and the one starts becoming the many. It sends out heat. The heat, in turn, thinks: let me be many, and sends out water. That's why, Uddalaka says, when a person is hot or grieving, they sweat or weep: water comes out of heat. The water thinks the same thought, and sends out food. That's why, wherever it rains, there's plenty to eat. Heat, water, food: the three basic stuffs everything else will be made of. Notice how close this is to the kitchen again. Fire, water, food. Uddalaka keeps building the biggest ideas out of the most ordinary things. And notice the motive. Nothing outside forces Being to make a world. It isn't lonely, or bored, or commanded. It simply thinks, let me be many. Hindu thinkers have spent centuries on that line. Some hear it as the one truly becoming the many. Others hear the one appearing as many while staying one. The text, for now, just tells the story, and leaves the rest for the lessons to come.
screen: `BEING ALONE, ONE WITHOUT A SECOND.` · `HOW COULD BEING COME FROM NOTHING?` · `IT THOUGHT: LET ME BE MANY.` · `HEAT, THEN WATER, THEN FOOD.` · then, large: `SAD EVA SOMYEDAM AGRA ASIT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice goes back to before. Sit and let the breath settle. Let the room fade: the sounds, the light, the chair. Let your thoughts thin out until there's very little: just the fact of being here. Rest there, in plain being. Then notice how, all on its own, something arises: a sound, a thought, a sensation. One becoming many, again. Let it come and go, and rest in being. The bell holds the time.

342.title: The three colors — red, white, black (6.4)
342.hook: look at a flame: the red is heat, the white is water, the black is food, and the 'fire' itself turns out to be a name
342.tomorrow: food, water, heat become mind, breath, speech
342.howItsDone: The idea that everything is woven of a few basic strands runs through later Hindu thought, including the three gunas of Samkhya and the Gita; some scholars see Uddalaka's three colors as an early forerunner of these ideas, though the link is debated.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: in the beginning, Being alone, one without a second. Your line was it thought: let me be many. Heat, then water, then food. What did you notice growing from one into many? Day three hundred forty-two.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING — LET ME BE MANY.`

segments.voice: Light a match and look closely at the flame. It isn't one color. There's a reddish glow, a bright whitish part, and a dark edge where the wick or the stick is burning down. Most of us just see fire, and blow it out before it reaches our fingers. Uddalaka, teaching his son, looks at the same flame and sees the whole creation story from yesterday, still going on, right there in the colors.
screen: `LIGHT A MATCH.` → `NOT ONE COLOR.` → `THE CREATION STORY, STILL GOING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Being became three things: heat, water and food. Now Uddalaka says Being entered into them with the living self, and gave them name and form, and wove each one together with the other two, so that everything is a braid of three. Then he points to a fire. The red color of fire is the form of heat. The white color is the form of water. The black color is the form of food, of earth. And then he says something startling: so the fireness of fire has gone. The change is only a name, a matter of words. The truth is the three colors. You've heard that phrase before. It's the clay line from two days ago, word for word, except now the pot is a flame. He does the same with the sun, the moon and lightning. Red, white, black, in each. Sun-ness, moon-ness, lightning-ness: names. The three are what's there. Then he adds something about the old teachers. The great householders of old, he says, knew this, and so they said: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or thought or known. Whenever they saw something red, they knew it as heat. White, as water. Black, as food. The point isn't really chemistry. Nobody's claiming this is how a modern lab would describe a flame. The point is a way of seeing. Behind the bright, separate things of the world, Uddalaka sees a few simple strands, and behind those strands, the one Being they came from. Look behind the colors, and the world gets simpler, not smaller.

343.howItsDone: Many Hindus treat food as sacred: it is often offered to God before eating, and traditions of mindful eating and dietary practice connect what one eats with the clarity of the mind.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three colors, red for heat, white for water, black for food. Your line was behind the colors. What did you see something made of? Today ends week two of year two. Day three hundred forty-three.
screen: `THE THREE COLORS — BEHIND THE COLORS.`

segments.voice: You know the version of yourself that hasn't eaten since breakfast and it's now four o'clock. Short temper. Foggy head. You read the same email three times. Someone hands you a sandwich, and ten minutes later you're a person again. Everyone knows that feeling, and most of us just call it being hungry. Nobody thinks of it as a lesson about the mind. Uddalaka built a lesson on it, and it may be the first recorded experiment in the Upanishads.
screen: `FOUR O'CLOCK, NO LUNCH.` → `THE SAME EMAIL, THREE TIMES.` → `A SANDWICH, AND YOU'RE BACK.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka tells his son what happens to the three stuffs once they're inside you. Food, when eaten, divides into three. The coarsest part leaves the body. The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind. Water, when drunk, divides the same way. The coarsest part leaves. The middle becomes blood. The finest becomes breath. Heat, when taken in, through oils and ghee, divides too. The coarsest becomes bone. The middle becomes marrow. The finest becomes speech. So mind is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat. Shvetaketu says, please, tell me more. So his father gives him an experiment. Don't eat for fifteen days. Drink water as you like, since breath is made of water and you'll need it. Shvetaketu fasts. Then he comes back, and his father says: recite the Vedas. And he can't. Nothing comes, sir. His father gives a picture: when a great fire has burned down to one ember the size of a firefly, it can't burn much. But add straw, and it blazes again. Go eat. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and now he can answer every question. The mind is made of food, my dear. Now the week, looked at from the top. Upakosala and the fires. The king's five fires. The proud son and the one question. The clay. Being alone, which thought, let me be many. The three colors. And today: food becoming mind. The Chandogya keeps refusing to separate the sacred from the stomach.
screen: `FOOD BECOMES FLESH AND MIND.` · `WATER, BREATH. HEAT, SPEECH.` · `FIFTEEN DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` · `THE EMBER AND THE STRAW.` · then, large: `THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices the ember. Sit and settle. Notice how your body feels right now: hungry, full, somewhere between. Notice your mind's brightness: sharp, foggy, tired. Without judging either, just see how they go together. Then think of the last thing you ate, and where it came from, and that some of it is now the attention you're paying to this moment. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Food. In Uddalaka's lesson, the finest part of food becomes mind, as the finest part of water becomes breath, and of heat, speech.
